lesson.title: Budgeting a Lifetime: Reproduction, Growth, and Survival Trade-offs
lesson.summary: A species' life history strategy, its typical age at first reproduction, number and size of offspring, parental investment, and lifespan, reflects evolutionary trade-offs that allocate limited energy in whatever way tends to maximize lifetime reproductive success.
lesson.body:
Every organism has a finite amount of energy and time, and every bit of that budget spent on one thing is a bit that cannot be spent on something else. Life history theory is the branch of ecology and evolutionary biology that studies how species have evolved to divide that limited budget among competing demands: growing larger, surviving to reproduce, producing many offspring versus a few well provisioned ones, and caring for offspring after they are born or hatched. The particular combination of traits a species has settled into, its age at maturity, number of reproductive events over a lifetime, offspring number and size, and degree of parental care, is called its life history strategy.

The central idea is trade-off. An organism that pours energy into producing a huge number of offspring typically cannot also provision each one generously or guard it closely, simply because the energy has to come from somewhere. An organism that invests heavily in a small number of offspring, feeding, protecting, or teaching them for an extended period, correspondingly cannot produce nearly as many. Neither strategy is objectively better: which one tends to be favored depends heavily on the mortality risks a species faces, which is exactly why life history strategies connect so directly to survivorship curves. A species with a Type III survivorship pattern, where the overwhelming majority of offspring die young regardless of what the parent does, tends to evolve toward producing very large numbers of offspring, since investing heavily in any single one offers little payoff when its odds of survival are so low no matter what. A species with a Type I pattern, where offspring that receive adequate care have a good chance of surviving to adulthood, can gain more from investing heavily in each one.

This is also where the concept of relative fitness comes in directly. Natural selection does not favor traits that simply maximize the number of offspring produced, or that simply maximize an individual's own survival. It favors whatever combination of traits, in a given environment, produces the greatest lifetime reproductive success relative to other individuals, accounting for the trade-offs involved. A strategy that produces many offspring but loses nearly all of them may achieve the same or lower fitness than a strategy that produces few offspring but ensures most of them survive.

A useful real contrast is the difference between semelparous and iteroparous reproduction. Pacific salmon are semelparous: after years spent growing in the ocean, they migrate upstream once, spawn a single massive batch of eggs, and then die shortly afterward, pouring essentially all of their remaining energy into that one reproductive event. Most birds and mammals, humans included, are iteroparous instead, reproducing repeatedly across multiple breeding seasons or years, which spreads reproductive investment out and hedges against the chance that any single reproductive attempt fails.

As with survivorship curves, it is worth resisting the temptation to sort every species neatly into one bucket or another. Life history traits form a continuum shaped by many interacting pressures, predation risk, resource availability, how predictable the environment is from year to year, and no species represents a pure version of any single strategy. That same continuum is the subject of the next chapter, which looks specifically at the ends of the spectrum ecologists commonly call r-selected and K-selected.
